metadata.name: Streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat, group A Streptococcus)
metadata.name_ar: التهاب الحلق العِقدي (البكتيري بالمكورات العقدية المجموعة A)
metadata.emergency_level: Routine — but recognise suppurative (quinsy) and non-suppurative (rheumatic fever) complications
metadata.severity: Usually self-limiting; antibiotics shorten illness and reduce complications/transmission

overview.short_description: Acute pharyngitis/tonsillitis caused by group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus, typically with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender cervical nodes WITHOUT cough, benefiting from antibiotics in higher-probability cases.
overview.detailed_description: GAS is the most important treatable bacterial cause of sore throat. It is distinguished from viral pharyngitis by clinical scoring and, where used, rapid antigen testing or culture. Antibiotics modestly shorten symptoms, reduce transmission, and prevent suppurative and (in at-risk populations) rheumatic complications. Overuse of antibiotics is avoided by treating higher-probability cases.
overview.pathophysiology: GAS adheres to and invades pharyngeal epithelium, producing local inflammation with exudate and tender lymphadenitis. Toxin production can cause scarlet fever (sandpaper rash). Immune cross-reactivity can (rarely) lead to rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
overview.etiology: Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes); spread by respiratory droplets and close contact.
overview.natural_history: Self-limiting over ~1 week even untreated; antibiotics shorten illness by ~1-2 days, reduce transmission, and lower complication risk.
overview.prognosis: Excellent with treatment; complications (quinsy, rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis) are uncommon, with rheumatic fever now rare in high-income settings.

prevalence.value: GAS causes roughly 5-15% of adult and up to ~20-30% of childhood sore throats.

incidence.value: Common, peaking in winter/spring; highest in children 5-15 years.

mortality.value: Negligible directly; serious outcomes via rare invasive disease or rheumatic complications.

epidemiology.age_groups: Predominantly children/adolescents (5-15 years); less common in young children <3 and adults.
epidemiology.geographic_distribution: Worldwide; rheumatic fever burden higher in low-resource settings.

risk_factors.pregnancy: Not a specific risk factor; affects antibiotic choice.
risk_factors.genetic_factors: Host susceptibility to rheumatic fever varies.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Prior rheumatic fever markedly increases importance of treating GAS.

chief_complaints.complaint: Sore throat with painful swallowing and fever

symptoms.symptom: Tender, enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes

symptoms.importance: A defining Centor criterion favouring strep
When present, strongly indicates GAS (scarlet fever)

negative_findings.why_important: These viral features make streptococcal infection much less likely (lower score)

negative_findings.finding: No trismus, uvular deviation, muffled voice, or drooling
negative_findings.why_important: Absence argues against peritonsillar abscess/airway emergency

history_questions.question: Do you have a cough or cold symptoms?
How high is your fever and how quickly did symptoms begin?
history_questions.why_ask: Fever is a scoring feature; rapid onset common

history_questions.question: Any rash, and has your tongue changed appearance?
history_questions.expected_answer: Usually no; if yes, supports GAS

history_questions.question: Any one-sided severe pain, trismus, drooling, or breathing difficulty?
History of rheumatic fever or significant heart valve disease?
history_questions.why_ask: Raises the threshold to treat and follow up

physical_examination.expected_finding: Erythema, exudate, tonsillar enlargement; check for asymmetry (quinsy)
Sandpaper rash / strawberry tongue if scarlet fever

laboratory_tests.test_name: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for GAS
laboratory_tests.indication: To confirm strep in higher-probability cases where testing is available/used
laboratory_tests.rule_out: Negative lowers probability; in children may warrant backup culture

laboratory_tests.indication: Confirmation/backup where RADT negative but suspicion remains (esp. children), or for surveillance
If glandular fever is a competing diagnosis
laboratory_tests.expected_result: Atypical lymphocytes / positive EBV serology in EBV

ecg.findings: May show conduction changes in acute rheumatic fever (rare complication).

other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Throat swab culture for GAS (reference standard)
other_diagnostic_tests.pcr: Molecular GAS tests available in some settings

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical probability by Centor/McIsaac or FeverPAIN, optionally confirmed by RADT or throat culture. GAS cannot be reliably diagnosed by examination alone; scoring +/- testing is used to guide antibiotics.

diagnostic_scores.value: Centor (1 point each): fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, ABSENCE of cough (McIsaac adds age adjustment). FeverPAIN (Fever, Purulence, Attend rapidly, Inflamed tonsils, No cough/coryza).

cutoff_values.value: Centor >=3 or FeverPAIN >=4 indicate higher GAS likelihood and support antibiotics/testing (NICE NG84).

differential_diagnosis.differences: Cough/coryza present, lower score, no exudate
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Do you have a cough and runny nose?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Young adult, marked fatigue, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly, prolonged
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Splenic rupture; airway obstruction; amoxicillin rash
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are you a young adult with weeks of fatigue and swollen glands?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Unilateral, trismus, muffled voice, uvular deviation
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is the pain one-sided with trismus?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Toxic, drooling, stridor, minimal oropharyngeal findings

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a cough or cold symptoms?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: No cough + fever + exudate + tender nodes -> higher GAS likelihood

diagnostic_questions.question: Is there a sandpaper rash or strawberry tongue?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Present -> strongly supports GAS; notify per local rules

next_best_question.current_situation: Sore throat with fever/exudate, no airway red flags
next_best_question.question: Do you have a cough/cold symptoms, and any rash or one-sided severe pain?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Viral features vs strep/scarlet features vs abscess features
next_best_question.branching_logic: Viral features -> avoid antibiotics; high score/scarlet -> antibiotics +/- testing; unilateral/airway signs -> urgent ENT

next_best_test.why: Estimates GAS probability to guide management

red_flags.finding: Stridor, drooling, or difficulty breathing/swallowing saliva
red_flags.immediate_action: Airway emergency — urgent ENT/anaesthetics (suspect epiglottitis); do not examine throat aggressively

red_flags.finding: Unilateral severe pain with trismus, muffled voice, uvular deviation
Signs of invasive GAS / streptococcal toxic shock (hypotension, rash, very unwell)
New joint pains, carditis features, or chorea weeks after infection
red_flags.immediate_action: Assess for acute rheumatic fever (especially at-risk populations)

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected peritonsillar abscess/deep-space infection; suspected invasive GAS disease.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Recurrent documented tonsillitis meeting tonsillectomy criteria; suspected rheumatic fever for specialist assessment.
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Airway compromise, streptococcal toxic shock, or acute rheumatic carditis.

late: Acute rheumatic fever (rare in high-income settings)

initial_management.supportive_care: Analgesia/antipyretics, fluids, rest; explanation and safety-net advice.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; NSAID; Phenoxymethylpenicillin; Macrolide. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG84.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Stay home while febrile / for ~24 hours after starting antibiotics to reduce spread; fluids and rest.
initial_management.follow_up: Safety-net for airway/deep-space signs, poor response, or complication features; notify scarlet fever per local public-health rules.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Antibiotics for higher-probability cases (Centor >=3/FeverPAIN >=4), systemically unwell, scarlet fever, or high complication risk: first-line phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5-10 days (per guideline); use a macrolide (e.g., clarithromycin) if penicillin-allergic. AVOID amoxicillin if EBV is possible (rash). Complete the course to reduce complications/transmission. Consider delayed prescribing in intermediate-probability cases.

patient_education.home_advice: Strep throat is a bacterial throat infection. Antibiotics can help when it's likely strep — take the full course. Painkillers and fluids ease symptoms, and you're much less contagious about a day after starting antibiotics. Seek urgent help for difficulty breathing or swallowing saliva, drooling, one-sided severe pain, or a widespread rash with feeling very unwell.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: التهاب الحلق العِقدي عدوى بكتيرية. قد تفيد المضادات الحيوية عندما يكون السبب بكتيرياً على الأرجح — أكمل الجرعة كاملة. مسكّنات الألم والسوائل تخفّف الأعراض، وتقلّ العدوى كثيراً بعد نحو يوم من بدء المضاد. اطلب المساعدة العاجلة عند صعوبة التنفّس أو بلع الريق، أو سيلان اللعاب، أو ألم شديد في جانب واحد، أو طفح منتشر مع توعّك شديد.
patient_education.prevention: Hand hygiene, avoiding close contact and sharing utensils while infectious.
patient_education.warning_signs: Difficulty breathing or swallowing saliva, drooling, one-sided severe throat pain with trismus, spreading rash with feeling very unwell, or new joint pains/breathlessness weeks later.

prevention.lifestyle: Hand/respiratory hygiene; stay home while infectious.
prevention.screening: Not routine; secondary prophylaxis (long-term penicillin) for those with prior rheumatic fever.

evidence.evidence_level: High for scoring-guided antibiotic use; modest symptomatic benefit and complication reduction from antibiotics.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_NG84; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
